content: Thermodynamics governs energy transformations and the direction of spontaneous processes. The First Law of Thermodynamics (conservation of energy) states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted between forms. In smartphones, electrical energy converts to chemical energy during charging, then to electrical energy during use, with some energy inevitably converting to heat in both processes. The Second Law states that entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases over timeâall real processes increase total entropy. This explains why batteries heat up during charging and use; some energy inevitably disperses as thermal energy, representing increased molecular disorder. Enthalpy (H) represents the total heat content of a system, while Gibbs free energy (G = H - TS) determines reaction spontaneityânegative ÎG indicates spontaneous processes. Battery charging has positive ÎG (non-spontaneous), requiring energy input, while discharging has negative ÎG (spontaneous), releasing energy. Efficiency losses in energy conversion follow the Carnot principle, explaining why batteries get warm and never deliver 100% of their stored energy as useful work. Fast charging increases entropy production rate (more heat) because rapid energy transfer creates more molecular disorder than gradual charging.

scenario.title: Smart Device Energy Lab
scenario.content: Students explore energy flows in a detailed virtual smartphone, focusing on battery charging and discharging processes. The simulation visualizes energy transformations at the molecular level, showing electrons moving through circuits and chemical reactions occurring within the battery. Heat generation appears as molecular vibrations and temperature color mapping. Students can adjust charging rates, usage patterns, and ambient conditions to see how these factors affect energy efficiency and heat production. Real-time graphs track energy input, useful output, and thermal losses. The simulation highlights the relationship between charge/discharge rates and heat generation, demonstrating why fast charging produces more heat than slow charging. Challenge scenarios task students with optimizing battery performance while managing thermal issues, teaching practical applications of thermodynamic principles.

hypothesis.description: Students will apply thermodynamic laws by analyzing energy transfers and transformations in electronic devices. They will predict how system changes affect energy efficiency and heat production, and explain why some energy is always lost as heat during energy conversion processes.
